newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Ramos aide says move afoot to extend term.
newsitem.headline: Ramos aide says move afoot to extend term.

text.p: A top Philippine government official has revealed plans to extend the term of President Fidel Ramos, provoking Vice-President Joseph Estrada to declare on Sunday he would lead a nationwide campaign against the move.
Analysts warned the plan could be sharply divisive and might rekindle fears that the country was in for autocratic rule akin to that of the late strongman Ferdinand Marcos.

Executive Secretary Ruben Torres said on Saturday that members of the president's People Power (Lakas) party favoured scrapping the constitutional provision limiting the president to one six-year term, and would try to convince Ramos to agree.
"If the demand is overwhelming, maybe he (Ramos) will bow to it," Torres told reporters. "Six years is really so short for a good president."
It was by far the strongest signal from the administration that Ramos, who will turn 69 next month, may still be in office in the 21st century.
Ramos has denied he is seeking another stint in office when his current term ends in June next year, but has initiated moves to amend the constitution to clip the wings of the Supreme Court.

Earlier this month, the court set aside the sale of the historic, government-owned Manila Hotel to a Malaysian firm and, under a "Filipino First policy", awarded it instead to a local company that had lost the public bidding.

Ramos had said the decision was a slap in the face to his privatisation programme, the cornerstone of his economic reform agenda. Last week he called for changes in the constitution to curb the power of what he called an "intrusive" Supreme Court.

Estrada, who has made no secret of his plans to seek the presidency and is widely regarded as the man to beat in the 1998 elections, said he would launch a nationwide campaign to oppose any charter changes.
"I have always supported President Ramos, but if he is seeking to change the constitution, then we will part ways. I cannot swallow it," Estrada said in an interview on a private radio station.
Elections for the president and vice-president are held separately in the Philippines and Estrada is not a member of Lakas. He belongs to the opposition Party of the Filipino Masses.
"Only the blind cannot see the signals that the president is determined to stay in office by executing a bloodless constitutional coup on himself," the Philippine Daily Inquirer said in an editorial.

"That's what President Marcos did. The only difference is that Marcos used martial law to deliver the coup, while President Ramos is executing his coup with the fig leaf of a constitutional amendment."

Marcos was in power for 20 years until he was dethroned by a popular people's movement in 1986. His successor, Corazon Aquino, included a presidential term limit in the new constitution to prevent any incumbent from staying too long in office.
The leftist umbrella group Nationalist Patriotic Alliance vowed to "storm the Congress" to thwart any attempts to tamper with the constitution.
"We will not give them peace," its secretary general Nathaniel Santiago told reporters.

Said political analyst Teodoro Benigno: "We are a democracy precisely because our leaders and our political parties...alternate peacefully to power. Disturb or disrupt that as President Marcos disrupted it when he declared martial law and you set loose a whirlwind where madmen will rule. Again."
